extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction writers, and students/critics of narrative craft
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for selecting and handling narrative method (first/third person, epistolary, authorial stance) so that a novel's subject is shown with the appropriate dramatic force and economy. Emphasizes when to let mind/action be dramatized rather than reported.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of first-person narration
rubrics_metrics.description: A personal narrator will do very well and may be extremely helpful, so long as the story is only the reflection of life beyond and outside him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use first-person when the narrator's role is to describe an external world (the narrator as onlooker/recorder). Avoid or be wary of first-person when the story's centre of gravity lies in the narrator's own inner life—then autobiography/report is insufficient because no man can completely objectify himself. Examples: Harry Richmond (Meredith) as recorder vs. David Copperfield where the subject is communal rather than internal. Anti-pattern: expecting a retrospective autobiographer to dramatize ongoing consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize internal life rather than rely on retrospective report
rubrics_metrics.description: When the man in the book is expected to make a picture of himself, a searching and elaborate portrait, the limit of first-person capacity is touched; his report of himself becomes a matter which might be strengthened by dramatization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer techniques that put the reader inside the protagonist's mind as it acts (showing thoughts 'in the act') rather than relying solely on a character's later account. Examples of effective dramatization: Dostoevsky's Raskolnikov and Henry James's Strether, where the reader experiences the mind's agitation directly. Anti-pattern: sole dependence on autobiographical narration for revealing complex, ongoing mental processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select a 'seeing eye' (point of view) suited to the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: Most novels postulate a point of view which is not that of the reader; the story requires a seeing eye — a selecting, interpreting, composing minister.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether the subject needs a particular viewpoint to be rendered (e.g., Vanity Fair requires a selecting eye). Choose the narrator or focalizer who best gathers and composes the material the novel must present. If no selecting eye is needed, pure drama (scene-on-stage) may suffice. The subject itself indicates the ideal point on the line from reporter to dramatist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer indirect/dramatic methods to direct authorial telling
rubrics_metrics.description: The more circuitous procedure on the part of the author produces a straighter effect for the reader; that is why, other things being equal, the more dramatic way is better than the less.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim to let people and action appear independently rather than be explained by the author. Use dramatization (showing) where possible to place the thing itself in view instead of recalling or explaining it. Example: Henry James's method of making a mind tell its own story without authorial exposition. Caveat: push toward drama only as far as the subject benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of method — do not over-treat the subject
rubrics_metrics.description: The method is to be pushed as far as the subject can profit by it, but no further. A story is damaged by too much treatment as by too little.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use dramatic or pictorial methods only to the degree that enhances the subject; avoid enriching a character's inner life unnecessarily if it will displace the novel's centre or obscure the subject (example: Dickens could have dramatized David's mind but would have misplaced the subject). Balance dramatization with restraint.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make the mind visible via surface behaviour and successive impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: The novelist represents the story by means of the movement that flickers over the surface of his mind. The impulses and reactions of his mood are the players upon the new scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When dramatizing thought, render it through its surface manifestations — momentary images, looks, tones, small actions — so the reader can infer inner states. Do not rely on extraneous exposition; let the 'passing images' and successive ripples of mind carry the narrative. This creates suspense and preserves dramatic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorial restraint — refrain from supplying privileged knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Henry James knows all there is to know of Strether, but he most carefully refrains from using his knowledge. He wishes us to accept nothing from him on authority — only to watch and learn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stepping in as an omniscient expositor when dramatization is possible. If the author begins to expound a character's inner substance, he risks misleading the reader (must 'let us into every secret') and destroys the dramatic suspense. Preserve the reader's position as observer rather than informant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the novel's central matter
rubrics_metrics.description: For any story there is an ideal point upon this line of progress towards drama, where the author finds the right method of telling the story. The point is indicated by the subject of the story itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let the nature of what you want to make plain (e.g., a mind in transformation vs. a chain of social events) determine whether to use first-person, third-person close, dramatization, or scenic presentation. Be deliberate: the subject dictates the appropriate narrative stance and degree of drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use epistolary/diary method to capture contemporaneous emotion (with limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Making a story out of a series of letters, or a running diary written from day to day, is an attempt to show a mind in action and to set the reader in the midst of it; it avoids throwing the subject into the past and preserves immediacy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ letters/diaries when the novel's subject is immediate emotion and you need the 'wheel of life' pulsing before the reader (example: Clarissa). But beware of practical drawbacks and verisimilitude strains: contrivances to keep correspondents apart and the artificiality of 'writing continually' can undermine credibility (Richardson's heavy shifts). Use this method sparingly and with awareness of its costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid letting the narrator obstruct access to active mind
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not let the hero come between us and his active mind, do not let the heroine stand in front of her emotions and portray them — unless for cause, for some needful effect that would otherwise be missed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that narrative vantage points do not place a barrier between reader and the life/mind at a story's centre. If a narrator's mediation dilutes immediacy or prevents dramatization of thought, prefer techniques that put the mind 'in front of the scene' (e.g., third-person presentation of consciousness). Exception: deliberate impairments can be used for specific effects (e.g., Barry Lyndon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve novelist's liberty to transcend immediate scene while dramatizing mind
rubrics_metrics.description: By dramatizing the mind, the novelist forfeits none of his special freedom; he is not constrained like the playwright to turn his story into dramatic action and nothing else.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when the mind is present and dramatized, the novelist may still provide panoramic vision, compress months into minutes, or use brief narrative summaries where appropriate. Use dramatization for immediacy while retaining the novelistic capacity for breadth and selective compression.

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate narrator choice (e.g., mystery constraints)
rubrics_metrics.description: In a tale of murder and mystery there is one man who cannot possibly be the narrator, and that is the murderer himself; for if he admits us into his mind at all he must do so without reserve, thereby betraying the secret that we ought to be guessing at for ourselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose narrators with regard to genre expectations and necessary suspense. For mysteries, avoid confined narrator choices that would eliminate the reader's opportunity to infer and discover. Use the narrator to preserve or reveal secrets according to the story's requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat the record of emotions so that they gain dramatic immediacy
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the record is one of emotions and sentiments, delicately traced and disentangled, it is not so easy to see how they may be exposed to an immediate view; the epistolary form or close contemporaneous reporting can provide a manner of meeting the difficulty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the subject is largely emotional interiority, choose forms (letters, diaries, close present-tense scenes, or surface dramatization) that keep the emotional struggle in the foreground and make the reader share the experience. Beware that some methods (like long correspondence) can exact heavy costs in plausibility; weigh benefits against practical narrative problems.
